How do you feel about these concepts for a system.

Basics

  • Experience points are earned based on how difficult a task should be. (Very Easy = 1, Easy = 2,... Very Hard = 5)
  • No levels, just skill points. Stealth is a skill, Melee is a skill, crafting is a skill, etc. (Fallout, Wasteland, Travellers, etc.)
  • Skills are limited to 10+related ability+luck.
  • Abilities are limited to 10+luck.
  • Luck has no limit, only increasingly difficult rolls.

The better your luck the better your chances to increase your natural abilities. The better your natural abilities the better your chances to increase your skills. If you are a lucky individual who is naturally gifted in dexterity you will have a better chance of increasing your stealth skill than a clumsy oaf with the luck of a footless rabbit.

Increasing Skills

  • You have the option of rolling to increase a skill after rolling a natural 20 on that skill.
  • You must spend experience points equal to your current skill.
  • Experience points are used in the attempt to increase a skill.
  • You have to beat your current skill with a roll of 1d10+ability+luck.
  • If you roll a 10 you keep half of your experience points.
  • If you roll a 01 you have to increase another skill before attempting this one again.
  • Ex. Increasing your stealth skill
  • * Stealth @ 12 / Dexterity @ 6 / Luck @ 2
  • * Meet or beat a 13 with 1d10+6+2
  • * Meet or beat a 13 with 1d10+8
  • * Meet or beat a 05 with 1d10
  • * Cost of 12xp

Increasing Abilities

  • You have the option of rolling to increase an ability after rolling a natural 20 on a related skill.
  • You must spend twice the experience of your current ability.
  • Experience points are used in the attempt to increase an ability.
  • You have to beat your current ability with a roll of 1d10+luck.
  • If you roll a 10 you keep half of your experience points.
  • if you roll a 01 you have to increase another ability before attempting this one again.
  • Ex. Increasing your dexterity ability
  • * Dexterity @ 6 / Luck @ 2
  • * Meet or beat a 7 with 1d10+2
  • * Meet or beat a 5 with 1d10
  • * Cost of 12xp

Increasing Luck

  • You have the option of rolling to increase luck after any natural 20.
  • You must spend three times the experience points of your current luck, minimum 1 to gain luck of 1.
  • Experience points are used in the attempt to increase luck.
  • There is no penalty for rolling all 1's and only one benefit from rolling all 6's.
  • You have to roll all 6's on a number of d6's equal to your next luck score.
  • Ex. Increasing your luck
  • * Luck @ 2
  • * Roll [6, 6, 6] on 3d6
  • * Cost of 9xp

My main concern would be that players would min-max the shit out of their characters. Hopefully the diminishing chances for success the higher your skill/ability/luck would lead to more balanced characters.

My assumption is that all players would spend some xp on getting luck of 1 (roll [6] on 1d6 and spend 1xp) or maybe luck 2 (roll [6, 6] pm 2d6 and spend 6xp). I cannot imagine many players actually going for luck 3 (roll [6, 6, 6] on 3d6 and spend 9xp). Similarly, I cannot see a player ignoring a basic survival skill that only costs 1xp and is almost guaranteed to pass.

I would probably use a double roll method. The player rolls once for themselves and the dm rolls in secret. If the player fails or thinks the DM rolled a 10 they could use the DM's roll.

I have Asperger's syndrome and you pretty much hit the nail on the head. Social interaction is a learned skill for people with Autistic Spectrum Disorders, not something that comes naturally. Plenty of people with ASD do learn social graces and how to better interact with people, but it's an academic pursuit more than an inherent desire. I was completely shit at interacting with people until my late teens because I didn't realize how important social interactions are in the real world.

I actually am completely unsure whether I have ASD or not. I have a TON of the symptoms, but a psychiatrist told me I don't exhibit them extremely enough to actually have it. That said, it was a military doctor and they're not the best. Anyway, regardless of whether I have it or not, I've always been drawn toward the logical rather than the emotional. I embrace philosophies and political beliefs that are logical, so much that I ignore any arguments that come from emotion. I am in touch with my emotions, but in a way that someone watching a TV show can understand the emotions of the characters. I feel like a spectator rather than someone taking part in it. It makes me a good counselor but I'm really awkward when I have to actually take part in social situations. People accuse me of "being a robot" whenever I have to weigh in on emotional stuff. I also have the uncanny ability to turn my empathy and emotions on and off, so I can give a shit about what people think when it's necessary and not give a single shit when I don't want to. It's kinda nice.

It's a tricky thing to diagnose because it's a spectrum disorder, but you very well could be on that spectrum. Different doctors may disagree over a particular diagnosis as well.

The way I usually put it is that a lot of what comes naturally to people are conscious decisions for me. I smile when I'm happy because I decide to smile, not because I feel like smiling. I understand that it's expected and natural behavior, so I emulate that.

It feels like everyone was born with an instruction manual I don't have access to, so I have to figure it out as I go. That doesn't mean people with ASD don't end up good at it, just that it takes a while and you pick up on different things at different rates.

Other symptoms can include a special and intense interest in one or two specific hobbies and being inherently uncomfortable with eye contact. When people hold a conversation, they rely on unconscious social cues to determine how long they maintain eye contact, when to look away, when they're starting to stare, etc. People naturally follow two tracks of a conversation without thinking about it.

People with ASD often aren't able to subconsciously follow that second track of social cues, so it's easier to listen when they "turn off" that second track by looking at something else while they listen. Trying to regulate eye contact and facial expressions often makes me tune out what someone is saying.

There are several potential symptoms that may or may not be present in an individual, and they're sometimes just more exaggerated traits of things that ordinary people have.

Before the Echo (formerly known as Sequence) was on Xbox Live Indie Games and now on PC is an RPG where you're basically player DDR except with three simultaneous stepcharts. Completing measures can increase mana, defend against attack, or cast spells, depending on which of the stepcharts you switch to, and you mix it up during the song. Kind of interesting, but plagued with a bit of grindiness and the Portal inspired "testing" theme looks even more derivative now than when it came out, but a pretty unique experience.

As far as breadth of mechanics, Audition is a dance game that has a huge number of game modes. It's also on Steam, but I'm not going to link it because the developers recently got caught providing in-game currency to players that left positive reviews. I used to play it years ago. It mostly resembles Bust a Groove (Bust a Move in Japan) where you have a sequence of directions to tap out and then hit space on the last beat of a measure. This base mechanic has a lot of variety, from insanely long sequences on really fast tracks, to "chance" where they mix in arrows that you have to hit the opposite to score, to group modes, to freestyle where you either memorize or start a sequence of steps and you have a lot of freedom in exactly what moves your character does. There is also more traditional timed tapping, couples modes where two players have to key in different arrows of the same sequence, and probably lots more stuff since I last played it maybe 8 years ago.
